summary: Describes several cryptographic algorithms for use with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), which is used to sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt message content. It replaces RFCs 2630 and 3211 for this purpose and was later updated by RFCs 5754 and 8702.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3370 gives implementations shared rules for using cryptographic algorithms with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS). These rules say how to identify each algorithm and encode its settings so systems can interpret protected messages consistently.

subtitle: The algorithm identifiers and parameter rules CMS implementations use to exchange protected messages.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax can sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt message content, but implementations need shared rules for identifying algorithms and encoding their parameters.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3370 defines conventions for digest, signature, key-management, content-encryption and message-authentication algorithms. For each algorithm, it identifies the CMS fields and parameter encodings to use.
tldr.outcome: If an implementation supports an algorithm described here, it MUST follow these conventions. RFC 3370 obsoletes Section 12 of RFC 2630 and RFC 3211, and the unit metadata lists RFC 5754 and RFC 8702 as updates.

today: RFC 3370 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes Section 12 of RFC 2630 and RFC 3211. The unit metadata lists RFC 5754 and RFC 8702 as updates.

sections.title: How This Document Fits with CMS
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) is used to sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt message contents. RFC 3370 describes conventions for using several cryptographic algorithms with CMS; it does not require every implementation to support every listed algorithm.

If an implementation chooses to support an algorithm in this document, it MUST use that algorithm as specified. CMS values use Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1) with Basic Encoding Rules (BER). Algorithm identifiers name the algorithms, and some also require parameters in a specified ASN.1 structure.

This document updates the algorithm conventions formerly in Section 12 of RFC 2630. RFC 3369 replaces the remaining parts of that earlier CMS document, allowing protocol and algorithm specifications to change separately.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS defines a format for protected messages. This RFC tells implementations how to name and encode several algorithms they may use with that format.

sections.title: Digest and Signature Algorithms
sections.content:
The digest algorithms covered are SHA-1 and MD5. Their identifiers appear in CMS digest fields, and digest values can also be inputs to signature algorithms. For SHA-1, parameters may be absent or NULL; implementations MUST accept both forms and SHOULD generate the form with parameters absent. For MD5, parameters MUST be present and contain NULL, although implementations MAY accept absent parameters.

The signature algorithms covered are DSA and RSA using PKCS #1 version 1.5. DSA MUST be used with SHA-1. Its signature contains two integers, r and s, encoded together in a Dss-Sig-Value structure. For DSA with SHA-1, the algorithm identifier's parameters MUST be absent.

Implementations that include RSA signatures MUST also implement SHA-1 and SHOULD support MD5. RSA signatures use one signature value. The supported RSA signature identifiers specified here require NULL parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: A digest produces a value from message content, and a signature uses a key to sign a digest. The RFC specifies which algorithm names and parameter encodings CMS uses for these operations.

sections.title: Getting the Content Key to Recipients
sections.content:
CMS supports four general ways to provide a content-encryption key to recipients: key agreement, key transport, a previously distributed symmetric key-encryption key, and a password-derived key-encryption key.

For key agreement, RFC 3370 specifies X9.42 Ephemeral-Static and Static-Static Diffie-Hellman. Both use version 3 and require a key-wrap algorithm for each content-encryption algorithm. Static-Static key agreement MUST include a user keying material value so that messages between the same sender and recipient produce different key-encryption keys.

For key transport, RSA PKCS #1 version 1.5 encrypts the content key. Symmetric wrapping can use Triple-DES or RC2. Password-based key management uses PBKDF2 to derive a key-encryption key; its parameters include a salt and an iteration count, and the salt MUST use the specified OCTET STRING form.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS needs a way to get the key for the message to each recipient. This RFC defines rules for deriving, agreeing on, transporting or wrapping that key.

sections.title: Encrypting Content and Checking Changes
sections.content:
For content encryption, the RFC specifies Triple-DES and RC2 in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode. Triple-DES applies three DES operations in sequence. Its algorithm parameters contain an initialization vector (IV) of exactly 8 octets.

RC2 CBC parameters contain an RC2 parameter version and an IV of exactly 8 octets. For effective key sizes of 40, 64 and 128 bits, the parameter-version values are 160, 120 and 58. The value 160 is encoded as two octets, 00 A0.

For message authentication, the RFC specifies HMAC with SHA-1. Implementations MUST accept its identifier with parameters absent or NULL, and SHOULD generate it with parameters absent.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption hides message content, while a message-authentication code helps detect changes. The RFC defines the algorithm identifiers and required settings for the listed methods.

sections.title: The Shared ASN.1 Definitions
sections.content:
Section 7 collects the algorithm identifiers, public-key types, signature-value types and parameter structures in an ASN.1 module named CryptographicMessageSyntaxAlgorithms. It includes definitions for DSA and RSA public keys, DSA signatures, key-wrap parameters, CBC parameters and PBKDF2 parameters.

The module imports the AlgorithmIdentifier type from the PKIX module and marks its definitions for export to other ASN.1 modules. This gives implementations a common formal source for the structures defined throughout the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The final section gathers the names and data structures from the RFC into one formal ASN.1 module. Other ASN.1 modules can import those definitions.

sections.title: Protecting Keys and Algorithm Choices
sections.content:
Implementations must protect private signing keys, key-management private keys, key-encryption keys, content-encryption keys and message-authentication keys. If these keys are compromised, attackers may impersonate a signer, disclose encrypted content or alter authenticated content.

Keys, IVs, one-time values and padding must be generated randomly. If key-encryption and content-encryption algorithms differ, the weaker algorithm determines the effective protection. The RFC therefore says key-encryption algorithms must be at least as strong as content-encryption algorithms.

The RFC also warns that RSA PKCS #1 version 1.5 encryption can be vulnerable to adaptive chosen-ciphertext attacks, especially in interactive systems that reveal decryption results. It advises implementers to keep algorithm choices modular because algorithms can weaken as cryptanalysis and computing capability improve.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping keys secret and generating unpredictable values are essential to these methods. A stronger content cipher cannot protect a message if its key is protected by a weaker key-encryption method.
